[Editors’ note: this article was originally rejected after discussions between the reviewers, but the authors were invited to resubmit after an appeal against the decision.]

Thank you for submitting your work entitled "Dynamic control of hippocampal spatial coding resolution by local visual cues" for consideration by eLife. Your article has been reviewed by a Senior Editor, a Reviewing Editor, and three reviewers. The following individuals involved in review of your submission have agreed to reveal their identity: Sara N Burke (Reviewer #1).

Our decision has been reached after consultation between the reviewers. Based on these discussions and the individual reviews below, we regret to inform you that your work will not be considered further for publication in eLife. Although potentially interesting, the results are not strong enough to support publication in eLife. Their novelty compared to previous results is not completely compelling, the interpretation is not entirely clear (e.g. presence of objects compared to enriched optic flow), and most importantly the results seem preliminary/ statistically weak in coming from very small numbers of animals in some analyses.

Reviewer #1:

The manuscript, "Dynamic control of hippocampal mapping resolution by local visual cues" by Bourboulou et al., documents the modulation of spatial coding by virtual 3-dimensional objects with a comprehensive analysis of firing properties of CA1 neurons in conditions with and without virtual objects. I have a few issues with the presentation of these data that would be helpful for the authors to address. First, throughout the Introduction and stated in the abstract the authors contend that, "whether hippocampal spatial coding resolution can be dynamically controlled within and between environments is unknown." This statement is false. In fact, there have been a number of studies showing that spatial coding resolution can be affected by behavioral/experimental parameters such as objects and active versus passive movement. Please see, Lee et al., 2012, Song et al., 2005, Terrazas et al., 2005 and Burke et al., 2011. The authors cite the Burke et al. (2011) paper but make no mention that this study also reported a decrease in place field size in the presence of objects, as well as an increase in the rate of theta phase precession. As it stands in the current presentation, the authors are upselling the novelty of their data.

A second major issue is how the statistics were conducted. It appears that cell number or place field number were the degrees of freedom for most analyses. Because multiple cells are recorded from the same animals, this is a nested design. In other words, multiple observations (cells) from a single subject (mouse) are treated like independent samples. The fact that many of the cells are from a common animal violates the statistical assumption that the observations are indeed independent. I refer the authors to Aarts et al., (2014) for an elegant description and meta-analysis of how such an approach can increase the chance of a Type I error. The data should be re-analyzed to account for the nested design of the experiment. Moreover, the authors do not report how many cells/fields were recorded from each mouse; so different animals could be making disproportionate contributions to the data.

Finally, the authors' use of the Hilbert transform to calculate theta phase is somewhat problematic. Hilbert imposes symmetry on the oscillation and it is known that theta is not symmetrical (Belluscio et al., 2012). This could lead to estimation errors for instantaneous phase that would obscure the quantification. At a minimum, the authors need to show that the shape of the theta oscillation (that is, the degree of asymmetry) did not vary between the object and no object conditions.

Reviewer #2:

In this paper, Bourboulou et al., show that the resolution of the hippocampal map is improved in the presence of 3D objects in the environment. They record hippocampal activity from head fixed mice running on virtual linear tracks with or without objects to show an improvement in spatial resolution and stability as well as improved theta phase precession.

While there are multiple major concerns with this paper, the biggest concern is the small number of experimental subjects per condition (**2**-3). More sessions per subject or more neurons per session cannot compensate for the possibility that the differences they saw could be the idiosyncrasies of individual subjects.

Major concerns:

1) Subsection “Low proportion of landmark vector cells in OT” "Because LV cells tend to systematically discharge near objects, these cells should discharge near the same object (s) in both back and forth trials."

This is not an accepted criterion to call a cell a LV cell. Both Deshmukh and Knierim as well as Geiller et al., papers, quoted by the authors, use the tendency to fire at multiple locations defined with respect to multiple objects to identify LV cells. The criteria in the present study merely identify bidirectional neurons. We know place fields tend to be unidirectional on 1D tracks. There's no reason why there can't be unidirectional LV cells on 1D tracks. Deshmukh and Knierim used 2D arenas, while Geuller et al., had 1D arenas, but unidirectional movement; neither of these studies have any information about bidirectionality of LV cells on 1D tracks.

Geiller et al., do refer to bidirectional predictive cells, "Indeed, it is worth noting that in a study 43 where local cues were laid on a linear track, place cells similar to LV cells were reported in significantly large numbers. These cells had bidirectional place fields that encoded in each direction an equidistant position ahead of a landmark, and were suggested to reflect view-invariant object information.", but are careful not to call these cells LV cells. In fact, the LV cell model by McNaughton et al., (1995), and the Collett et al., (1986) observations that model was supposed to explain would not predict this activity, since the animals (and the LV cells in the model) need to keep track of allocentric direction as well as distance from the landmark.

It is possible that the LV cells exhibit this bidirectional behavior in linear tracks, but there needs to be a comparison of behavior of LV cells in 2D and 1D before this bidirectional behavior gets labelled as LV.

Furthermore, this may not be the only possible representation of LV cell activity. Do the authors notice place fields equidistant from two or more objects in the same cell more often than expected by chance? That is the more classic LV cell behavior reported in Deshmukh and Knierim as well as Geiller et al., papers.

Subsection “Low proportion of landmark vector cells in OT” "In the track with objects, LV represented only 6.79% of all place cells. This corresponds to the proportion of LV cells recorded in area CA1 in the presence of real objects (Deshmukh and Knierim, 2013)."

This is an incorrect characterization of Deshmukh and Knierim results. McNaughton et al., (1995) posted that place cell vectors could be bound to one or more landmarks ("typically one, occasionally two, rarely more than two"). The percentage reported in Deshmukh and Knierim is that of LV cells with vectors bound to two or more landmarks; the paper had no means to characterize LV cells bound to a single land marks (which would be virtually indistinguishable from place cells with single place fields in absence of object manipulation). Thus, the low proportion of LV cells reported is the limitation of the method, not the actual proportion of LV cells, which is expected to be much higher.

Discussion section "the lateral entorhinal cortex where LV cells were first discovered (Deshmukh and Knierim, 2011)".

Deshmukh and Knierim (2011) did not report LV cells in LEC.

2) The papers switches between parametric and nonparametric tests, based on whether the data were normally distributed and had equal variance. While this is acceptable practice for individual tests, it is impossible to compare statistical significance across different comparisons of same quantities in the paper if one uses parametric tests while the other uses nonparametric tests. It will be better to use nonparametric tests throughout. In addition, median and range need to be reported when using nonparametric stats; mean and SEM reported in the paper are inappropriate. Conversely, reporting medians and range is inappropriate when performing parametric statistics (e.g. the box plots in Figure 1E).

3) Subsection “Effects of local visual cues on spatial coding resolution2: "similar rate of reward collections (OT: 1.70} 0.29 rewards/minute, n = 9 recording sessions in 3 mice; OT: 1.15} 0.09 rewards/minute" and "average running speed (OT: 14.1} 2.12 cm/s, n = 9 recording sessions in 3 mice; OT: 16.8} 1.58 cm/s, n = 5 recording sessions in 2 mice"

How is the average running speed for the without object track lower than that for OT (with object track), while the average reward rate is lower for OT? Do the average speed calculations exclude stationary periods? Do the OT mice sit longer at reward? More importantly, do they slow down at objects?

If they do slow down at objects, can this explain better spatial resolution/stability/place field dispersion in neural code near objects? i.e., can this be simply explained by slower speeds or longer time spent, ensuring better sampling of space near objects, and thus more (and less variable if the speeds at other locations vary more than those near objects) firing rate estimates at these locations than locations away from objects?

4) Subsection “Effects of local visual cues on spatial coding resolution” "There was a tendency for place field width (calculated on complete fields) to be lower in the track with objects (OT: 111 51.5} 3.33 cm, **n = 15 place fields**;".

This is a very small number of place fields (15) to be compared quantitatively. This ties in with the issue of small sample size (number of mice) used throughout the paper. Curiously, the authors report a greater number of place fields in the same without object condition elsewhere: subsection “Effects of local visual cues on spatial coding resolution” "Accordingly, spatial information (in bit/spike), a measure independent of place fields' detection (Skaggs et al., 1993) was very low in the track without object (0.06} 0.01 bit/spike, n = 48 place cells)". Place cells are defined as cells with at least 1 place field (subsection “Effects of local visual cues on spatial coding resolution”). Is that because most of these 48 cells don't meet the criterion of "complete place field" for even 1 field? Doesn't this make the definition of a "place cell" a bit too permissive? Clearly 31 of these fields were good enough for end track vs on track comparison (subsection “Virtual 3D objects improve spatial resolution locally”).

5) Subsection “Local visual cues improve hippocampal population coding accuracy” "We used the spike trains from all pyramidal 192 cells recorded (i.e., both the spatially modulated and nonspatially modulated cells) and compared decoded positions with actual positions of the animal in the virtual linear tracks."

Does using only the spatially modulated cells improve decoder accuracy? An explicit comparison of decoding accuracy using a matched number of spatially modulated cells is crucial, in addition to the "active cell" ensemble data presented here.

In continuation of the above point, subsection “Local visual cues improve hippocampal population coding accuracy”: "In both cases, downsampling was performed to equalize the number of cells used for decoding between the two conditions (20 active cells)."

Even after downsampling to 20 cells, most cells are place cells for with object but not place cells for without object condition. Matched number of place cells will complement this analysis.

6) The paper has no data to prove that it is the 3D nature of objects rather than their localized sensory information that is responsible for improvement in spatial representation.

7) Subsection “Recording procedure” "**On the day before recording**, animals were anesthetized (induction: isoflurane 3%; maintenance: Xylazine/Ketamine 10/100 mg/Kg supplemented with Buprenorphine 0.1 mg/Kg) and a craniotomy was drilled above one hippocampus (centered on a location -2 mm posterior and} 2.1 mm lateral from bregma)."

These lines and the rest of the paragraph in the methods give an impression that there was a single acute recording session per animal, the it is clear from the results that there were multiple recording sessions per animal (e.g. subsection “Effects of local visual cues on spatial coding resolution” "n = 5 recording sessions in 2 mice").

Each of these sessions included exposure to with and without object conditions: Subsection “Recording procedure” "All mice (n = 8) experienced first the familiar environment (either OT, OT or EOT) for around 20 back and forth trials. For mice trained in OT or OT (n = 3 and 2, respectively), this first exploration was followed, after 3 minutes of free running with the screens displaying a black background, by exploration of a new environment, identical to the previous one except for the presence of the three 3D objects (objects were added for mice trained in OT and removed for mice trained in OT) for another 20 consecutive back and forth trials." This means that the later sessions (session 2 onwards) had previous exposure to the "novel" condition; was there an effect of increasing familiarity on the neural response?

It is not clear from the description if the probes were fixed in one position on the first day of recording and reused over multiple days, or if they were inserted at different locations on different days. If they were at the same location, the statistics will be affected by the inflated degrees of freedom while recording from the same (or significantly overlapping) set of neurons over multiple days.

8) Discussion section "Nevertheless, End-track fields had a low spatial information content and stability when compared to fields recorded in OT (but similar to On-track fields recorded in the same maze). This argues against increased spatial coding resolution at these locations and further suggests a possible dissociation between overrepresentation and increased spatial coding resolution."

Or, it could simply be explained by the confusion caused by dissociation between the animal's movement and the arena caused by "teleportation" at the ends of the track.

9) Subsection "Effects of virtual objects in a visually enriched environment": This section lacks an essential control with enriched environment without objects.

10) Subsection “Virtual reality environments” "Outside the maze walls, two large 3D columns were positioned on each side (dimensions 8 x 8 x 47 cm; positions 58 and 143 cm from end wall) to provide additional visual cues.

While 58cm column position is close to an object, 143 cm position is not; there appears to be an enhancement in local stability near 143cm. But these columns are 3D, so doesn't detract from the overall analysis – just compounds the interpretation of this specific experiment. Is the reported improvement in neural code really due to an enrichment or merely an increase in number of discrete landmarks available to the animals?

Reviewer #3:

In this paper, the authors record hippocampal neurons as mice explore virtual reality environments that vary in their presence or absence of visual objects. They find that the resolution, defined as the number, spatial stability and scale, or place cells increases in the presence of visual objects. They go on to show that visual objects also enhance temporal coding, with theta phase precession emerging to a larger degree in the object rich compared to object poor environment. These results have interesting implications for our understanding of how hippocampal circuits dynamically change their coding properties based on the visual features available to the animal. In general, the experiments and the analyses in this paper are rigorously performed. The authors convincingly demonstrate a number of coding differences in hippocampal activity between the two environments. However, I do have concerns regarding interpretation, controls and sample size.

1) Interpretation and controls: I'm not certain to what degree the increased place cell resolution is driven by an 'object' per say versus the availability of improved optic flow sources. The use of a visually rich track with objects goes part way to addressing this issue but does not account for the fact that the optic flow from objects may carry more information than the optic flow from the walls, due to the proximity of the objects to the mouse. Moreover, the appropriate control here would be to record in the visually rich environment in the absence of the objects. It is possible that the presence of the objects induces a ceiling effect (perhaps coding cannot be further improved). More convincing to me would be that the visually rich environment without objects did not improve coding to the same degree as the presence of objects.

2) Sample size: Unless I misunderstood something, the number of place cells out of the total number of cells seems surprisingly low (48 and 103 out of 1124), which is concerning. I also have some concern about the number of mice used in the OT track (n = 2); while the overall cell number is large, I worry that this sample size is too small in terms of individual animals. Moreover, the session number is also rather small in some cases.

[Editors’ note: what now follows is the decision letter after the authors submitted an appeal.]

Thank you again for choosing to send your work entitled "Dynamic control of hippocampal spatial coding resolution by local visual cues" for consideration at eLife. Your article and your letter of appeal have been considered by a Senior Editor, a Reviewing Editor, and the original reviewers. We would happy to consider a new submission along the lines of your appeal, but please take note of the specific points below:

- Specifically, the authors would need to include the controls in a revised version, as well as the additional animal. The authors should redo the statistics taking into account the nested design after adding more data as indicated.

- In addition, the authors also need to substantially overhaul the writing of the entire manuscript to reflect the claims they make in the rebuttal/appeal.

For example, they state in the rebuttal, "We classified a cell as a LV cell if it responded either to multiple objects (having place field in the same object zones in back and forth trial) or to a single object (if they in addition code for that object's identity)." The entire LV cells section (subsection “Low proportion of landmark vector cells in OT”) does not mention anything about object identity being used for LV detection. Neither does the LV cells section (subsection “Landmark Vector cells detection”). The results do mention responding to the same object in both direction as a criterion, but that is not object identity, as a neuron firing bidirectionally for all objects will also be classified as LV cell.

- The resubmission will have to also deal with related issues, like the claims about percentages of cells that are landmark vector cells and how they compare with the other papers, definition of LV cells as bidirectional cells without confirming their LV nature in 2D environments etc.

claims.claim: Place fields' spatial dispersion was decreased when objects were added.
claims.source: Place fields' spatial dispersion and out/in field firing ratio were decreased (Z = 3.55, p=0.0004 and Z = 1.87, p=0.06, respectively, two-tailed WRS test; Figure 4D and F).
claims.evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis and shown in Figures 4D and 4F.

claims.claim: Out/in field firing ratio was decreased when objects were added.
claims.source: Place fields' spatial dispersion and out/in field firing ratio were decreased (Z = 3.55, p=0.0004 and Z = 1.87, p=0.06, respectively, two-tailed WRS test; Figure 4D and F).
claims.evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis and shown in Figures 4D and 4F.

claims.claim: Removing objects decreased the proportion of place cells.
claims.source: On the other hand, removing objects decreased the proportion of place cells (from 71.1 ± 5.54% to 34.9 ± 10.9%, n = 8 sessions in three mice; t5 = 5.54, p=0.001, two-tailed paired t-test; Figure 4A and C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis and shown in Figures 4A and 4C.

claims.claim: Removing objects decreased the spatial information and stability.
claims.source: The spatial information and stability were decreased by this manipulation (Z = 2.27, p=0.02 and Z = 4.51, p<10−5, respectively, two-tailed WRS test; Figure 4E and G), while place field out/in field firing ratio and dispersion were increased (Z = −2.01, p=0.04 and Z = −3.06, p=0.002, respectively, two-tailed WRS test; Figure 4D and F).
claims.evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis and shown in Figures 4E and 4G.

claims.claim: Removing objects increased place field out/in field firing ratio and dispersion.
claims.source: The spatial information and stability were decreased by this manipulation (Z = 2.27, p=0.02 and Z = 4.51, p<10−5, respectively, two-tailed WRS test; Figure 4E and G), while place field out/in field firing ratio and dispersion were increased (Z = −2.01, p=0.04 and Z = −3.06, p=0.002, respectively, two-tailed WRS test; Figure 4D and F).
claims.evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis and shown in Figures 4D and 4F.

claims.claim: After object removal, local stability was not significantly higher in OZ compared to ØZ.
claims.source: After object removal, local stability was not significantly higher in OZ (OZ: 0.24 ± 0.02, n = 60 bins of 2 cm, 30 in each direction) compared to ØZ (0.24 ± 0.02, n = 100 bins of 2 cm, 50 in each direction; Z = 0.19, p=0.85, two-tailed WRS test; Figure 4I).
claims.evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis and shown in Figure 4I.

claims.claim: The effects of local visual cues on place cells' coding observed between familiar tracks can be reproduced with instantaneous objects manipulation.
claims.source: We conclude that the effects of local visual cues on place cells' coding observed between familiar tracks can be reproduced with instantaneous objects manipulation.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the objects manipulation experiments.

claims.claim: When objects were added in the empty track, map similarity was significantly higher for the second trial in the new condition.
claims.source: When objects were added in the empty track, map similarity was significantly higher for the second trial in the new condition (t-1 vs t + 2, n = 598 and n = 608 pyramidal cells, respectively; n = 5 sessions in three mice; Z = 7.18, p<10−9; Kruskall-Wallis one-way test with post-hoc Bonferroni correction) and then stayed higher from this second trial on (t + 2 vs t + 3, n = 608 and n = 612 pyramidal cells, respectively; n = 5 sessions in three mice; Z = 1.10, p=1, Kruskall-Wallis one-way test with post-hoc Bonferroni correction).
claims.evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis.

claims.claim: When objects were removed from the familiar track with objects, map similarity dropped already for the first trial in the new condition.
claims.source: Conversely, when objects were removed from the familiar track with objects, map similarity dropped already for the first trial in the new condition (t-1 vs t + 1, n = 744 and n = 743 pyramidal cells, respectively; n = 8 sessions in three mice; Z = 8.80, p<10−15, Kruskall-Wallis one-way test with post-hoc Bonferroni correction) and stayed lower from this first trial on (t + 1 vs t + 2, n = 743 and n = 720 pyramidal cells, respectively; Z = 0.17, p=1, Kruskall-Wallis one-way test with post-hoc Bonferroni correction).
claims.evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis.

claims.claim: The hippocampus can rapidly adapt its spatial coding resolution to local visual cues available in the environment.
claims.source: Thus, the hippocampus can rapidly adapt its spatial coding resolution to local visual cues available in the environment.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the dynamic analysis of map similarity.

claims.claim: Object-responsive cells tend to discharge systematically near several objects present in the environment.
claims.source: Newly activated place cells in OT could correspond to object responsive (OR) cells, which have been recorded in the hippocampus of freely moving rats (Deshmukh and Knierim, 2013). These cells tend to discharge systematically near several objects present in the environment.
claims.evidence: This is based on a citation to previous work.

claims.claim: In the track without objects no OR cell was detected.
claims.source: In the track without objects no OR cell was detected.
claims.evidence: This is a direct statement of the analysis results.

claims.claim: In the track with objects, OR cells represented only 2.07% of all place cells.
claims.source: In the track with objects, OR cells represented only 2.07% of all place cells.
claims.evidence: This is a direct statement of the analysis results.

claims.claim: The vast majority of newly activated place cells in the presence of objects does not correspond to OR cells.
claims.source: We conclude that the vast majority of newly activated place cells in the presence of objects does not correspond to OR cells.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the OR cell analysis.

claims.claim: The percentage of active cells was not affected by the presence of different patterns along the track.
claims.source: The percentage of active cells was not affected by the presence of different patterns along the track (OT, 54.64 ± 4.79%, n = 8 sessions in three mice; PØT, 53.63 ± 3.45%, n = 6 sessions in two mice; p=1, one-way Anova test with post-hoc Bonferroni correction; Figure 5C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis and shown in Figure 5C.

claims.claim: The percentage of place cells among active cells tended to be greater in PØT than in ØT.
claims.source: The percentage of place cells among active cells tended to be greater than in ØT (ØT, 18.71 ± 4.33%, n = 7 sessions in three mice; PØT, 42.16 ± 10.58%, n = 5 sessions in two mice; p=0.093, one-way Anova test with post-hoc Bonferroni correction).
claims.evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis showing a trend.

claims.claim: The percentage of place cells in PØT was significantly lower than in OT.
claims.source: Also, the percentage of place cells in PØT was significantly lower than in OT (OT, 71.11 ± 5.54%, n = 8 sessions in three mice; p=0.024, one-way Anova test with post-hoc Bonferroni correction; Figure 5B–D).
claims.evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis and shown in Figures 5B-D.

claims.claim: Place fields were uniformly distributed along the track enriched with patterns.
claims.source: Interestingly, place fields were uniformly distributed along the track enriched with patterns (n = 16 spatial bins of 10 cm; p=0.23, test for non-uniformity; Figure 5B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by statistical testing and shown in Figure 5B.

claims.claim: Local 2D visual cues are sufficient to set place fields' position.
claims.source: This suggests that local 2D visual cues are sufficient to set place fields' position.
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from the uniform distribution of place fields in PØT.

claims.claim: Place field width was significantly decreased in PØT compared to ØT.
claims.source: Place field width was significantly decreased in PØT compared to ØT (ØT, 51.46 ± 3.34 cm, n = 15 place fields; PØT, 41.51 ± 1.17 cm, n = 138 place fields; Z = 2.62, p=0.026, Kruskall-Wallis one-way test with post-hoc Bonferroni correction).
claims.evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis.

claims.claim: Place field dispersion was significantly reduced in PØT compared to ØT to a level comparable to OT.
claims.source: Accordingly, place field dispersion was significantly reduced compared to ØT to a level comparable to OT (ØT, 5.95 ± 0.45 cm, n = 48 place cells; PØT, 4.57 ± 0.21 cm, n = 157 place cells; Z = 2.88, p=0.011, Kruskall-Wallis one-way test with post-hoc Bonferroni correction; Figure 5E).
claims.evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis and shown in Figure 5E.

claims.claim: Inter-trial firing stability was significantly higher in PØT compared to ØT but significantly lower than in OT.
claims.source: Inter-trial firing stability, while significantly higher in PØT compared to ØT (ØT, 0.12 ± 0.01, n = 48 place cells; PØT, 0.19 ± 0.01, n = 157 place cells; Z = 3.72, p=0.0005, Kruskall-Wallis one-way test with post-hoc Bonferroni correction), was significantly lower than in OT (OT, 0.28 ± 0.01, n = 193 place cells; Z = 5.02, p<10−4, Kruskall-Wallis one-way test with post-hoc Bonferroni correction; Figure 5F).
claims.evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis and shown in Figure 5F.

claims.claim: Local 2D visual cues can improve place fields stability to a certain extend without reaching the level of stability observed in the presence of 3D virtual objects.
claims.source: We conclude that local 2D visual cues can improve place fields stability to a certain extend without, however, reaching the level of stability observed in the presence of 3D virtual objects.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the comparison of PØT with ØT and OT.

claims.claim: The ratio of place cells' out-of-field versus in-field firing was lower in PØT compared to ØT but still significantly higher than in OT.
claims.source: The ratio of place cells' out-of-field versus in-field firing was lower in PØT compared to ØT (ØT, 0.65 ± 0.02, n = 48 place cells; PØT, 0.53 ± 0.02 cm, n = 157 place cells; Z = 3.38, p=0.002, Kruskall-Wallis one-way test with post-hoc Bonferroni correction) but still significantly higher than in OT (OT, 0.46 ± 0.01, n = 193 place cells; Z = 3.02, p=0.007, Kruskall-Wallis one-way test with post-hoc Bonferroni correction; Figure 5G).
claims.evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis and shown in Figure 5G.

claims.claim: Spatial information content was higher in PØT compared to ØT but still significantly lower than in OT.
claims.source: Accordingly, spatial information content was higher in PØT compared to ØT (ØT, 0.056 ± 0.01, n = 48 place cells; PØT, 0.16 ± 0.02, n = 157 place cells; Z = 4.09, p=0.0001, Kruskall-Wallis one-way test with post-hoc Bonferroni correction) but still significantly lower than in OT (OT, 0.25 ± 0.02, n = 193 place cells; Z = 2.73, p=0.018, Kruskall-Wallis one-way test with post-hoc Bonferroni correction; Figure 5H).
claims.evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis and shown in Figure 5H.

claims.claim: Local 2D visual cues can enhance the proportion of place cells among active cells and place cells' coding accuracy but to a lower extend compared to 3D virtual objects.
claims.source: Altogether these results indicate that local 2D visual cues can enhance the proportion of place cells among active cells and place cells' coding accuracy but to a lower extend compared to 3D virtual objects.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the comparison of PØT with ØT and OT.

claims.claim: Local stability in OZ was significantly higher in OT compared to PØT.
claims.source: Finally, local stability in OZ was significantly higher in OT compared to PØT (OT-OZ: 0.52 ± 0.02; PØT-OZ: 0.39 ± 0.016, n = 30 spatial bins of 2 cm for both; Z = 4.85, p<10−5 two-tailed WRS test; Figure 5I).
claims.evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis and shown in Figure 5I.

claims.claim: Decoding accuracy in OZ was significantly higher in OT compared to PØT.
claims.source: Accordingly, the same effect could be observed for the decoding accuracy (OT-OZ: 0.07 ± 0.02; PØT-OZ: 0.03 ± 0.01, n = 30 spatial bins of 2 cm for both; Z = −5.83, p<10−8 two-tailed WRS test; Figure 5J) in agreement with a strong influence of 3D objects on spatial coding resolution.
claims.evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis and shown in Figure 5J.

claims.claim: The percentage of active cells was not increased by visually enriching the environment.
claims.source: The percentage of active cells was not increased by visually enriching the environment (OT, n = 5 sessions in two mice; EOT, n = 5 sessions in three mice; Z = −0.1, p=1, two-tailed WRS test; Figure 6C) nor was the percentage of place cells (OT, n = 5 sessions in two mice; EOT, n = 5 sessions in three mice; t8 = −1.38, p=0.20, two-tailed unpaired t-test; Figure 6B–D).
claims.evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis and shown in Figure 6C.

claims.claim: The percentage of place cells was not increased by visually enriching the environment.
claims.source: The percentage of active cells was not increased by visually enriching the environment (OT, n = 5 sessions in two mice; EOT, n = 5 sessions in three mice; Z = −0.1, p=1, two-tailed WRS test; Figure 6C) nor was the percentage of place cells (OT, n = 5 sessions in two mice; EOT, n = 5 sessions in three mice; t8 = −1.38, p=0.20, two-tailed unpaired t-test; Figure 6B–D).
claims.evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis and shown in Figures 6B-D.

claims.claim: Place fields were uniformly distributed along the track in the visually rich environment.
claims.source: However, place fields were uniformly distributed along the track in the visually rich environment (n = 16 spatial bins of 10 cm; p=0.23, test for non-uniformity), thus not clustered around objects as in the visually poor environment (Figure 6B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by statistical testing and shown in Figure 6B.

claims.claim: Local visual cues are important to set place fields' position.
claims.source: This suggests that local visual cues are important to set place fields' position (Renaudineau et al., 2007).
claims.evidence: This is an inference supported by a citation.

claims.claim: All other attributes of place fields were not significantly different between OT and EOT.
claims.source: However, all other attributes of place fields were not significantly different between the two environments (OT, n = 103 place cells; EOT, n = 132 place cells; out/in field firing ratio: Z = 0.57, p=0.57; Spatial info: Z = 0.42, p=0.67; Dispersion: Z = −1.88, p=0.06; Stability: Z = −0.06, p=0.95; two-tailed WRS test for all; Figure 6E–H).
claims.evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis and shown in Figures 6E-H.

claims.claim: There was still a significant effect of objects in the visually enriched environment in OZ versus ØZ in terms of local stability.
claims.source: When looking at local stability of firing rates, we still observed a significant effect of objects in the visually enriched environment in OZ versus ØZ (OZ, n = 60 spatial bins of 2 cm; ØZ: n = 100 spatial bins of 2 cm; Z = −2.46, p=0.014, two-tailed WRS test; Figure 6I).
claims.evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis and shown in Figure 6I.

claims.claim: Positions near objects were decoded with a better accuracy than positions further away in the visually enriched environment.
claims.source: Interestingly, positions near objects were also decoded with a better accuracy using a Bayesian decoder than positions further away in the visually enriched environment (OZ: 0.07 ± 0.004, n = 30 spatial bins of 2 cm; ØZ: 0.057 ± 0.003, n = 50 spatial bins of 2 cm; Z = −4.49, p=0.004, two-tailed WRS test; Figure 6J).
claims.evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis and shown in Figure 6J.

claims.claim: In the presence of local visual cues, hippocampal spatial coding is not further improved by visually enriching the environment.
claims.source: Altogether these results suggest that in the presence of local visual cues, hippocampal spatial coding is not further improved by visually enriching the environment.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the comparison of OT and EOT.

claims.claim: Place fields locations are influenced by additional visual cues along the track.
claims.source: However, place fields locations are influenced by additional visual cues along the track.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the uniform distribution of place fields in EOT.

claims.claim: Despite a homogeneous distribution of place field locations, 3D objects could still locally influence hippocampal population decoding accuracy.
claims.source: Interestingly, despite a homogeneous distribution of place field locations, 3D objects could still locally influence hippocampal population decoding accuracy.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the decoding analysis in EOT.

claims.claim: Theta phase precession is thought to further increase spatial coding resolution.
claims.source: This phenomenon, called theta phase precession, is thought to further increase spatial coding resolution because different locations within the place field that are difficult to distinguish based on firing rate alone can be accurately separated when phase is taken into account.
claims.evidence: This is based on established knowledge in the field.

claims.claim: Increased spatial resolution in the temporal domain would correspond to increased slope of the phase versus position relationship for identical field sizes.
claims.source: In the temporal domain, increased spatial resolution would thus correspond to increased slope of the phase versus position relationship for identical field sizes.
claims.evidence: This is a logical inference about what increased temporal resolution would entail.

claims.claim: The mean frequency of the field theta oscillation was not significantly different when mice were running in the track with or without objects.
claims.source: The mean frequency of the field theta oscillation was not significantly different when mice were running in the track with or without objects (ØT: 6.79 ± 0.12 Hz, n = 9 sessions in three mice; OT: 6.59 ± 0.33 Hz, n = 8 sessions in two mice; Z = 1.26, p=0.20, two-tailed WRS test) but was lower than that reported for mice navigating in real linear tracks (Middleton and McHugh, 2016).
claims.evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis and comparison with literature.

claims.claim: The power of theta oscillation was not significantly different between ØT and OT.
claims.source: The power of theta oscillation (theta index see Materials and methods section) was also not significantly different (ØT: 3.31 ± 0.23, n = 9 sessions in three mice; OT: 3.38 ± 0.16, n = 8 sessions in three mice; t15 = 0.26, p=0.79, two-tailed unpaired t-test).
claims.evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis.

claims.claim: Theta frequency was not modulated by running speed of the animal in ØT.
claims.source: Theta frequency was not modulated by running speed of the animal in ØT (r = 0.02 ± 0.02, n = 9 sessions in three mice; Figure 7—figure supplement 1A,C) as previously observed in virtual linear tracks when only distal cues are present (Ravassard et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This is supported by data analysis and shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1A,C, and is consistent with previous findings.

claims.claim: Theta frequency-speed modulation was significant in OT.
claims.source: Theta frequency-speed modulation was, however, significant in OT (r = 0.08 ± 0.03, n = 8 sessions in three mice; t15 = -1.44, p=0.17, two-tailed unpaired t-test; Figure 7—figure supplement 1A,C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by data analysis and shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1A,C.

claims.claim: Theta amplitude was similarly modulated by running speed in both conditions.
claims.source: Theta amplitude was similarly modulated by running speed in both conditions (ØT: r = 0.07 ± 0.03, n = 9 sessions in three mice; OT: r = 0.03 ± 0.02, n = 8 sessions in three mice; t15 = 0.08, p=0.43, two-tailed unpaired t-test; Figure 7—figure supplement 1B,D).
claims.evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis and shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1B,D.

claims.claim: The proportion of active putative pyramidal cells with significant theta modulation was not different between conditions.
claims.source: The proportion of active putative pyramidal cells with significant theta modulation was not different between conditions (ØT: 92.24%, n = 361 active cells; OT: 91.97%, n = 299 active cells; χ2 = 0.01, df = 1, p=0.89, Chi-Square test).
claims.evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis.

claims.claim: The coupling of spikes to theta oscillation was not significantly different between conditions in terms of preferred phase.
claims.source: The coupling of spikes to theta oscillation was also not significantly different between conditions in terms of preferred phase (ØT: 203.91°±2.6, n = 361 active cells; OT: 191.17°±2.87, n = 299 active cells; p=0.07, circular Kruskal-Wallis; Figure 7—figure supplement 2A,B) and strength (mean resultant vector length ØT: 0.18 ± 0.006, n = 361 active cells; OT: 0.19 ± 0.009, n = 155 active cells; Z = −1.63, p=0.1, two-tailed WRS test; Figure 7—figure supplement 2A,C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis and shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2A,B.

claims.claim: The coupling of spikes to theta oscillation was not significantly different between conditions in terms of strength.
claims.source: The coupling of spikes to theta oscillation was also not significantly different between conditions in terms of preferred phase (ØT: 203.91°±2.6, n = 361 active cells; OT: 191.17°±2.87, n = 299 active cells; p=0.07, circular Kruskal-Wallis; Figure 7—figure supplement 2A,B) and strength (mean resultant vector length ØT: 0.18 ± 0.006, n = 361 active cells; OT: 0.19 ± 0.009, n = 155 active cells; Z = −1.63, p=0.1, two-tailed WRS test; Figure 7—figure supplement 2A,C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis and shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2A,C.

claims.claim: The percentage of fields with significant and negative correlation between phase and position was high in the track with objects but low in the empty track.
claims.source: The percentage of fields with significant (p<0.05) and negative correlation between phase and position (i.e. precessing fields) was high in the track with objects (40.22%), comparable to that observed in real linear tracks in mice but low in the empty track (7.46%; χ2 = 26.57, df = 1, p<10−6 compared to OT, Chi-Square test).
claims.evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis.

claims.claim: The correlation between phase and position was significantly different from zero for place cells recorded in the track with objects but not for those recorded in the track without objects.
claims.source: Accordingly, the correlation between phase and position was significantly different from zero for place cells recorded in the track with objects (r = −0.14 ± 0.018, n = 177 fields; p<10−14, one sample sign-test; Figure 7A and B) but not for those recorded in the track without objects (r = 0.15 ± 0.024, n = 15 fields; p=0.30, one sample sign-test; Figure 7A and B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis and shown in Figures 7A and 7B.

claims.claim: Phase precession slopes were negative and significantly different from 0 for cells recorded in the track with objects but not in the track without objects.
claims.source: Moreover, phase precession slopes (calculated on normalized place field sizes) were negative and significantly different from 0 for cells recorded in the track with objects (−2.00 ± 0.17 rad/U, n = 177 fields; p<10−14, one sample sign-test; Figure 7C) but not in the track without objects (1.82 ± 0.44 rad/U, n = 15 fields; p=0.3, one sample sign-test; Figure 7C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis and shown in Figure 7C.

claims.claim: Local visual cues are important for proper theta phase precession in the hippocampus.
claims.source: Altogether, these results suggest that local visual cues are important for proper theta phase precession in the hippocampus.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the theta phase precession analysis.

claims.claim: There was a strong correlation between theta phase and physical distance in the presence of virtual 3D objects but not otherwise.
claims.source: Our analysis revealed a strong correlation between theta phase and physical distance in the presence of virtual 3D objects (OT: R = 0.39, n = 629 pairs in three mice; p<10−24, Pearson correlation; Figure 7E,F) but not otherwise (ØT: R = 0.21, n = 28 pairs in three mice; p=0.26, Pearson correlation; Figure 7E,F).
claims.evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis and shown in Figures 7E and 7F.

claims.claim: Local visual cues are important for temporal coding in the hippocampus beyond theta phase precession.
claims.source: These results show that local visual cues are important for temporal coding in the hippocampus beyond theta phase precession.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the theta timescale spike coordination analysis.

claims.claim: Spatial coding resolution was increased in the presence of local visual cues through an increase in the proportion of spatially selective place cells among active cells and enhanced place fields' spatial selectivity and stability.
claims.source: We found that spatial coding resolution was increased in the presence of local visual cues through an increase in the proportion of spatially selective place cells among active cells but also enhanced place fields' spatial selectivity and stability.
claims.evidence: This is a summary of the main findings stated in the Discussion.

claims.claim: The effects of local visual cues on spatial coding resolution were most prominent in the vicinity of local cues and dynamic upon their manipulations.
claims.source: These effects were most prominent in the vicinity of local cues and dynamic upon their manipulations.
claims.evidence: This is a summary of the main findings stated in the Discussion.

claims.claim: Local sensory cues proved to be important for temporal place cell coding such as theta phase precession and theta timescale spike coordination.
claims.source: Local sensory cues also proved to be important for temporal place cell coding such as theta phase precession and theta timescale spike coordination.
claims.evidence: This is a summary of the main findings stated in the Discussion.

claims.claim: Spatial resolution can be improved by pooling information across neurons.
claims.source: Spatial resolution can be improved by pooling information across neurons (Wilson and McNaughton, 1993).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation.

claims.claim: Local visual cues could dramatically increase the number of place cells among active cells by a threefold factor.
claims.source: We found that local visual cues could dramatically increase the number of place cells among active cells (by a threefold factor).
claims.evidence: This is a summary of the experimental findings.

claims.claim: An increase in the quantity/quality of sensory cues in an environment will enhance the number of place cells coding that environment according to sensory-based models.
claims.source: Using sensory-based models of place cells activation (Hartley et al., 2000; Strösslin et al., 2005; Barry et al., 2006; Sheynikhovich et al., 2009) one can predict that an increase in the quantity/quality of sensory cues in an environment will enhance the number of place cells coding that environment (Geva-Sagiv et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This is a prediction based on models cited in the literature.

claims.claim: Previous studies using local enrichment with multimodal sensory cues or real objects reported only weak or no effects on dorsal hippocampal cell activity.
claims.source: However, previous studies using local enrichment with multimodal sensory cues or real objects reported only weak or no effects on dorsal hippocampal cell activity.
claims.evidence: This is a summary of previous findings in the literature.

claims.claim: One study recording in rats navigating between cue-rich and cue-poor parts of the same track reported no effect on the proportion of place cells or on the density of place fields.
claims.source: One study recording in rats navigating between cue-rich and cue-poor parts of the same track reported no effect on the proportion of place cells or on the density of place fields. Furthermore, population vector analysis did not reveal a better disambiguation of nearby locations in the cue-rich part of the track compared to the cue-poor suggesting similar spatial coding resolution (Battaglia et al., 2004).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to Battaglia et al., 2004.

claims.claim: Other studies found no overall increase of place cells proportion in 2D environment containing real objects nor a specific bias for place cells to fire near the objects.
claims.source: Other studies found no overall increase of place cells proportion in 2D environment containing real objects nor a specific bias for place cells to fire near the objects (Renaudineau et al., 2007; Deshmukh and Knierim, 2013).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: One possibility to explain the lack of recruitment of additional cells in previous studies could be a high recruitment rate of the dorsal hippocampus even in the 'cue poor' condition due to the presence of uncontrolled local cues.
claims.source: One possibility to explain the lack of recruitment of additional cells in these studies could be a high recruitment rate of the dorsal hippocampus even in the 'cue poor' condition due to the presence of uncontrolled local cues (Ravassard et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors and supported by a citation.

claims.claim: Studies so far have revealed an homogeneous allocation of place fields in space in a given environment.
claims.source: However, studies so far have revealed an homogeneous allocation of place fields in space (Muller et al., 1987; Rich et al., 2014) in a given environment.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: The proportion of object-responsive cells is generally low in the dorsal hippocampus (between 6 and 8%).
claims.source: However, the proportion of these cells is generally low in the dorsal hippocampus (between 6 and 8%) which is in line with the fact that places near real objects are not overrepresented at the population level.
claims.evidence: This is based on established knowledge in the field.

claims.claim: The proportion of object-responsive cells may be underestimated and vary depending on the recording location along both the proximo-distal axis and radial axis.
claims.source: We note, however, that this proportion may be underestimated and vary depending on the recording location along both the proximo-distal axis and radial axis (Geiller et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation.

claims.claim: The distal part of CA1, closer to the subiculum, is more heavily innervated by the lateral entorhinal cortex where OR cells were first discovered.
claims.source: For example, the distal part of CA1, closer to the subiculum, is more heavily innervated by the lateral entorhinal cortex where OR cells were first discovered (Deshmukh and Knierim, 2011) and which is believed to feed information about the 'what' visual stream to the hippocampus (Knierim et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations.

claims.claim: Extracellular recordings specifically targeting the distal CA1 area in the intermediate hippocampus reported an increased proportion of place cells with smaller place fields in the presence of objects.

results.result: Virtual 3D objects globally enhanced hippocampal spatial coding resolution. The proportion of place cells increased from 19% to 71% in the presence of objects (C39-C40), with fields concentrated in the central track (C42). Objects improved place field stability (C46: p<10⁻¹⁰), reduced spatial dispersion (C45: p=0.01), decreased out-of-field firing (C49: p<10⁻⁷), and increased spatial information content (C50: p<10⁻⁷).
results.evaluation: Multiple converging measures with strong statistical significance demonstrate that 3D objects enhance spatial coding. The claims are internally consistent, with appropriate statistical tests (WRS, t-tests) and clear effect sizes. Sample sizes are adequate (n=3 mice per condition, 48-193 place cells), and the findings align across different metrics of spatial coding quality.

results.result: Virtual 3D objects locally enhanced spatial coding resolution in their vicinity (Object Zones, OZ). Place field density was significantly higher in OZ versus ØZ (C53: p=0.002), with smaller field widths (C54: p<10⁻⁵), reduced dispersion (C55: p<10⁻⁴), increased local stability (C56: p<10⁻⁶), and higher spatial information (C57: p=0.03). The out-of-field firing ratio effect was more global (C58, C60).
results.evaluation: The local analysis demonstrates spatial specificity of object effects with strong statistical support. The distinction between local effects (field density, size, stability) and global effects (out-of-field firing) is well-documented. The spatial binning approach (2-10 cm bins) is appropriate for the 2m track, and the non-uniform distribution test (C52: p=0.017) validates the spatial clustering.

results.result: Overrepresentation of place fields at track ends in ØT was not associated with increased spatial coding resolution. End-track fields showed no improvement in out-of-field firing ratio (C62: p=0.83), stability (C63: p=0.26), and paradoxically lower spatial information than on-track fields (C64: p=0.008).
results.evaluation: This negative result is important for distinguishing overrepresentation from increased coding resolution. The statistical comparisons are appropriate, and the finding that end-track fields have lower spatial information despite higher density argues against reward-related enhancement of spatial coding in this paradigm.

results.result: Population-level decoding analysis confirmed that objects improved spatial coding accuracy both globally and locally. Decoding error was nearly two-fold larger without objects (C66: p<10⁻³⁶), and decoding accuracy was three-fold lower (C67: p<10⁻⁵⁴). Local analysis showed significantly better decoding in OZ versus ØZ (C71: p<10⁻⁶), even when using fewer cells from OT than ØT (C69).
results.evaluation: The Bayesian decoding analysis provides strong population-level validation of single-cell findings. The drop-cell approach (C68-C69) controls for differences in place cell proportions, strengthening the conclusion. The 150ms time windows and leave-one-out cross-validation are appropriate methodological choices. Convergence with FRV decoding method adds robustness.

results.result: Object manipulations produced rapid, dynamic changes in spatial coding resolution. Adding objects instantaneously increased place cell proportion from 21.6% to 75.0% (C74: p<10⁻⁵), with 40.3% of cells becoming spatially modulated (C75). Removing objects reversed these effects (C83-C85). Map similarity analysis showed changes stabilized by the second trial after adding objects (C88) and immediately after removing objects (C89).
results.evaluation: The manipulation experiments provide strong causal evidence for object effects on spatial coding. The rapid timescale (1-2 trials) distinguishes these effects from slower learning-related changes. The bidirectional manipulation (adding and removing objects) strengthens causal inference. Sample sizes are adequate (n=5 and n=8 sessions for adding/removing), and statistical tests are appropriate (paired t-tests for within-session comparisons).

results.result: 2D wall patterns (PØT) provided intermediate enhancement of spatial coding between ØT and OT. Place cell proportion in PØT (42.16%) was between ØT (18.71%) and OT (71.11%), with uniform field distribution (C98: p=0.23). Stability, spatial information, and local decoding accuracy in PØT were significantly better than ØT but worse than OT (C102, C105, C107-C108).
results.evaluation: The graded effect across three conditions (ØT < PØT < OT) supports the hypothesis that local visual cue quality/dimensionality affects spatial coding resolution. The uniform distribution in PØT versus clustered distribution in OT suggests 2D cues can set field positions but 3D cues provide additional local enhancement. Statistical comparisons use appropriate post-hoc corrections (Bonferroni) for multiple comparisons.

results.result: Visual enrichment (EOT) did not further improve spatial coding beyond OT. Place cell proportions and field attributes were not significantly different between OT and EOT (C109-C110, C113). However, field distribution became uniform in EOT (C111), and objects still locally improved stability and decoding accuracy in OZ versus ØZ (C114-C115).
results.evaluation: This result suggests a ceiling effect for spatial coding enhancement, where additional distal visual cues provide diminishing returns once local 3D objects are present. The persistent local effect of objects in EOT (C114-C115) despite uniform field distribution indicates objects influence both field placement and local coding quality. The lack of differences in most metrics (C113) is well-supported statistically.

results.result: Local visual cues were essential for theta phase precession. In OT, 40.22% of fields showed significant phase precession with negative correlation (r=-0.14±0.018, p<10⁻¹⁴) and slopes (-2.00±0.17 rad/U, p<10⁻¹⁴). In ØT, only 7.46% of fields precessed (p<10⁻⁶ vs OT), with no significant phase-position correlation (C130: p=0.30). Theta frequency, power, and spike coupling were not significantly different between conditions (C121-C122, C126-C128).
results.evaluation: The theta phase precession analysis is rigorous, using spatially stable trials in ØT to control for stability differences. Multiple analysis methods (Hilbert transform, waveform-based, single-trial) converge on the same conclusion. The lack of differences in basic theta properties (C121-C128) rules out confounding explanations. The unit-LFP shift analysis provides independent confirmation. Sample sizes are adequate (177 fields in OT, 15 in ØT for SST).

results.result: Local visual cues enabled theta timescale spike coordination. Strong correlation between theta phase and physical distance was observed in OT (R=0.39, n=629 pairs, p<10⁻²⁴) but not ØT (R=0.21, n=28 pairs, p=0.26). This demonstrates that local cues are important for temporal coding beyond phase precession.
results.evaluation: The theta sequence analysis examines spike timing relationships between cell pairs with overlapping place fields, providing a population-level measure of temporal coding. The strong correlation in OT and lack thereof in ØT is well-supported statistically. However, the small number of pairs in ØT (n=28) reflects the low proportion of place cells in that condition, which could limit power for detecting weaker effects.

results.result: The experimental setup used head-fixed mice running on a wheel in a 2m virtual linear track with distinct wall patterns and reward zones at extremities. Mice performed similarly in ØT and OT conditions (reward rate: p=0.59; running speed: p=0.64). A total of 1021 neurons were recorded from CA1, with comparable proportions of active cells between conditions (p=0.14).
results.evaluation: The experimental design is well-described and appropriate for the research question. The virtual reality setup allows precise control of visual cues while maintaining behavioral engagement. Similar task performance between conditions (C36-C37) rules out motivation or attention differences as confounds. The comparable proportion of active cells (C38) indicates objects don't simply increase overall excitability. Sample sizes (n=3 mice per condition, 1021 total neurons) are adequate for the analyses performed.

results.result: Object-responsive (OR) cells, which fire near multiple objects, were rare in this study. No OR cells were detected in ØT, and only 2.07% of place cells in OT were classified as OR cells. This indicates that the majority of newly activated place cells in OT do not correspond to OR cells.
results.evaluation: The OR cell analysis addresses an important alternative explanation for increased place cell numbers near objects. The low proportion (2.07%) is consistent with previous literature reporting 6-8% in dorsal hippocampus. The classification criteria (bidirectional firing near same objects) are appropriate. However, the analysis could be limited by the specific definition used and the virtual nature of the objects.

results.result: The introduction establishes that flexible navigation relies on hippocampal cognitive maps (C1), with place cells providing the neural substrate (C9-C10). Dynamic control of spatial coding resolution could be important for navigation (C11), as mapping all space at high resolution would be computationally expensive (C13). Previous work shows place cell coding varies with behavioral conditions (C15-C16) and that local sensory cues could be instrumental in setting spatial coding resolution (C26).
results.evaluation: These claims provide appropriate background and motivation for the study. They are well-supported by citations to foundational and recent literature. The logical progression from established knowledge (C1, C9-C10) through computational considerations (C13) to the specific hypothesis (C26) is clear and well-justified. These are primarily literature review claims that set up the experimental work.

results.result: The discussion synthesizes findings and contextualizes them within existing literature. Key points include: (1) local visual cues dramatically increased place cell numbers (threefold), exceeding predictions from previous studies with real objects (C139-C143); (2) the effects are more compatible with improved spatial coding resolution than object-responsive cell activation (C155-C156); (3) overrepresentation can be dissociated from increased coding resolution (C157-C160); (4) the results complement previous VR studies showing distal cues alone are insufficient (C162-C163).
results.evaluation: The discussion appropriately interprets the findings in light of previous work. The comparison with Burke et al. 2011 (C149-C152) is particularly insightful, noting that while both studies found increased place cells with objects, the current study shows local increases in place cell density despite smaller fields. The acknowledgment of limitations (virtual vs. real objects, C153-C154) is appropriate. The mechanistic speculation is reasonable but clearly identified as such.

results.result: The discussion proposes several mechanisms for how objects improve spatial coding: (1) objects as stable reference points for path integration (C164-C165); (2) higher sensory resolution of local cues (C166-C167); (3) attentional modulation (C169), though task performance was similar between conditions (C170); (4) objects as noise is ruled out by poor decoding in ØT (C171-C172). For temporal coding, the discussion notes that phase precession was reduced without local cues (C173) but restored with objects (C174), and that the relationship between theta-speed modulation and phase precession is complex (C183-C185).
results.evaluation: The mechanistic discussion is appropriately speculative while being grounded in the data and previous literature. The ruling out of the noise hypothesis (C171-C172) is data-driven. The comparison with Ravassard et al. 2013 regarding theta-speed modulation (C183-C184) appropriately acknowledges complexity rather than forcing a simple interpretation. The discussion of phase precession mechanisms is cautious, noting that "future studies are needed" rather than overinterpreting the current findings.

results.result: The discussion concludes that local visual cues induce both global and local rescaling of spatial coding (C190), which could be computationally beneficial for large-scale navigation (C191-C195). In the wild, rodents travel long distances through varied terrain (C191), and mapping everything at high resolution would be costly (C192). The ability to map important locations at high resolution while using lower resolution for transit routes could be advantageous (C195), with resolution depending on local sensory information (C196).
results.evaluation: This functional interpretation is reasonable speculation based on the findings. The computational argument (C192-C195) is logical and supported by citations. The connection to natural behavior (C191) provides ecological validity. However, the study doesn't directly test navigational accuracy or memory, so the functional benefits remain hypothetical. The claim appropriately uses conditional language ("could be") rather than asserting proven benefits.
